title: The Prado in two hours: a route to the essentials, and which door to use
subtitle: Two floors, three painters who matter most, and one loop through the building that does not double back.
excerpt: A two-hour route through the Prado in Madrid: Bosch, the dark Goya, the main gallery, Las Meninas and El Greco, with the door to use and what each kind of ticket includes.
secondary_keywords: what to see at the Prado

meta_title: The Prado in two hours: a route to the essentials
meta_description: A two-hour route through the Prado: Bosch, Goya, the main gallery, Las Meninas, El Greco. Which door to use and what each ticket includes.

featured_image.alt: The main façade of the Prado Museum in Madrid, with the statue of Velázquez in front of its columns

content_html:
[place attraction="museo-del-prado" city="madrid"]

In November 1936, four months into the Civil War, bombs fell on the Prado. The galleries were already being emptied. Over the following weeks the best paintings in the building were crated, loaded onto lorries and driven to Valencia, later to Catalonia, and in the last winter of the war across the French border and on to Geneva. Las Meninas made the journey with them.

They came home by train in the first days of September 1939, just as another war was beginning around them. Since then the pictures have hardly moved, which is good news for a visitor in a hurry: the Prado is a museum where you can know in advance what you want and walk straight to it. Two hours are enough for the essentials, if you take them in the right order.

Why the Prado is easier than it looks

The Prado is not an encyclopaedia of art. It is the private collection of the Spanish kings, opened to the public in 1819 in a building that had been designed for a museum of natural history. The kings bought what they liked and kept buying it, so the museum is deep, not wide: no one has more Velázquez, more Goya, more Bosch or more Titian under one roof.

That gives you a simple plan. Three painters carry the visit, and they hang on two floors of one long building. The route below starts on the ground floor, climbs once and ends near the way out.

Which door to use

The doors of the Prado are named after painters, and they do different jobs.

  • The Goya door, at the north end, is where the ticket offices are. If you have no ticket, this is your line.
  • The Jerónimos door, at the back of the building beside the church of San Jerónimo, is normally the way in for visitors who already hold a ticket.
  • The Murillo door, at the south end facing the Botanical Garden, is generally kept for groups.

The grand front on the avenue, behind the statue of Velázquez, is not an entrance. Everybody passes a security check, and backpacks and umbrellas go to the cloakroom. Take the free paper plan: rooms are renumbered and rehung from time to time, and the plan is always current.

The north end of the building, the Goya door, where the ticket offices are. Photo: Discasto, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The route, stop by stop

1. Bosch (ground floor, north side)

Start with the early Flemish rooms. The Garden of Earthly Delights is a triptych painted around 1500: Eden on the left, a hell lit by fires on the right, and between them a crowd of naked figures, giant birds and outsized fruit that nobody has ever fully explained. Philip II collected Bosch and hung this one in his monastery palace of El Escorial. A few steps away is Rogier van der Weyden's Descent from the Cross, where the grief on ten faces is painted with a precision that still stops people.

The Garden of Earthly Delights: Eden on the left, hell on the right. Photo: Museo Nacional del Prado, via Wikimedia Commons.

2. The dark Goya (ground floor, south end)

Walk the length of the ground floor. Around 1820 Goya, old and deaf, painted fourteen scenes straight onto the walls of his house outside Madrid, for nobody but himself. They were cut from the plaster and moved to canvas in the 1870s. The Black Paintings include Saturn devouring his son and a dog alone against an empty sky. Close by hang his two canvases of the rising against Napoleon's troops, The Second of May 1808 and The Third of May 1808, both painted in 1814.

The Third of May 1808, painted by Goya in 1814. Photo: Museo Nacional del Prado, via Wikimedia Commons.

3. The court Goya (first floor, south end)

Go up one floor and you meet the same man thirty years younger: The Family of Charles IV, a royal portrait that flatters nobody, and the two Majas, the same woman on the same couch, dressed and undressed.

4. The main gallery (first floor)

The long central gallery runs the length of the building under a glass roof. Walk it slowly northwards: Titian's portrait of Charles V on horseback at Mühlberg, and Rubens at full size.

5. Las Meninas (first floor, room 12)

The large oval room off the middle of the gallery belongs to Velázquez. Las Meninas, painted in 1656, is more than three metres high: the five-year-old Infanta Margarita, her maids, a dog, and the painter himself at his easel, looking out at whoever stands where you are standing. In the mirror on the back wall are the king and queen. Stay ten minutes, then look at the same painter's court dwarfs and jesters, to whom he gave the dignity he gave to kings.

Las Meninas, 1656. The painter is on the left, looking at you. Photo: Museo Nacional del Prado, via Wikimedia Commons.

6. El Greco, on the way out (first floor, north end)

The last rooms before the stairs hold El Greco: long bodies, cold light, and The Nobleman with his Hand on his Chest. From here you go down to the exit.

What the tickets include

  • A museum ticket is entry, nothing more. The route above is enough to go with it.
  • A ticket with a masterpieces audio tour adds a guide that plays in the partner's app on your own phone and leads you from room to room. Bring earphones.
  • A ticket with a city sights audio tour sounds similar and is not: the commentary is for a walk through Madrid, and the listing says there is no audio inside the museum.
  • A masterpieces audio tour on its own is commentary only. You buy your entry somewhere else.

These are the Prado tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="museo-del-prado" match="prado" limit="6"]

When to go, and two rules

  • The Prado is open every day of the week, Mondays included, which is rare for a museum of its size.
  • The first hour of the morning is the calmest. For many years the last two hours of each day have been free of charge, and the line for them starts early and runs round the building. If you only have two hours, a paid morning slot is the better bargain.
  • Photography is not allowed in the galleries. The guards do enforce it.
  • Picasso's Guernica is not here. It hangs in the Reina Sofía, a fifteen-minute walk south.

Hours and free periods change. The current ones are on our page for the Prado Museum.

From here

The Retiro park begins five minutes uphill, behind the church of San Jerónimo, and the Royal Botanical Garden is next door to the south. If you have room for more painting, the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum is across the avenue and the Reina Sofía closes the triangle. See what else there is to do in Madrid, or fit the city into a longer route with the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Emilio J. Rodríguez Posada, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

faqs.q: Can you see the Prado in two hours?
faqs.a: You can see its best-known works in two hours with a fixed route: Bosch and the Black Paintings of Goya on the ground floor, then Goya, the main gallery, Las Meninas and El Greco on the first floor.

faqs.q: Where is Las Meninas in the Prado?
faqs.a: On the first floor, in room 12, the large room off the middle of the central gallery, with other works by Velázquez around it.

faqs.q: Which entrance should I use at the Prado?
faqs.a: Visitors who already hold a ticket normally go in by the Jerónimos door, at the back of the building. The ticket offices are at the Goya door, at the north end.

faqs.q: Is Guernica in the Prado?
faqs.a: No. Guernica by Picasso is in the Reina Sofía museum, about fifteen minutes on foot from the Prado.

faqs.q: Is the Prado open on Mondays?
faqs.a: Yes. The Prado opens every day of the week, with shorter hours on Sundays and public holidays. Check the current hours before your visit.

title: Seville Cathedral and the Giralda: what the ticket includes, and how the climb works
subtitle: One ticket covers the church, the tower and a second church across town. The tower has ramps, not stairs.
excerpt: What a ticket to Seville Cathedral covers, why the Giralda needs no ticket of its own, how the climb up its 35 ramps works, and what is sold separately.
longtail_phrases: is the Giralda included in the Seville Cathedral ticket
how many steps to climb the Giralda
is there a lift in the Giralda
where is Columbus buried in Seville Cathedral
how long does Seville Cathedral take
meta_title: Seville Cathedral and Giralda: ticket and tower climb
meta_description: What the Seville Cathedral ticket includes, how the climb up the 35 ramps of the Giralda works, what to see inside and what is sold separately.

featured_image.alt: Seville Cathedral with the Giralda bell tower rising behind it, seen from the street on a bright day

content_html:
[place attraction="seville-cathedral" city="seville"]

For a century and a half after the Christian conquest of Seville in 1248, the city's cathedral was its old mosque, with an altar where the prayer niche had been. By 1401 the building was failing, and the cathedral chapter voted to replace it. The words handed down from that meeting are a boast: let us build a church so large that those who see it finished will take us for madmen.

They did. The work took about a century and produced the largest Gothic church in the world. But the builders kept two pieces of the mosque: its courtyard, and its minaret, which became the bell tower. That is why a visit here is two visits in one, and why people ask before booking whether the tower is a second ticket and what the climb is like.

The vaults of the cathedral, begun in the first years of the fifteenth century. Photo: Adam Jones, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What the ticket covers

A general ticket to Seville Cathedral includes more than its name says:

  • The cathedral: the five naves, the chapels, the sacristies and the treasury rooms with their paintings.
  • The Giralda. The climb is part of the same ticket. There is nothing extra to buy for the tower.
  • The Court of the Orange Trees, the courtyard of the mosque, through which you leave.
  • The Church of El Salvador, a large baroque church about ten minutes' walk to the north, built on the site of an earlier mosque. It has long been sold together with the cathedral, and far fewer people go.

Entry is for a set time, and at busy periods the day sells out.

How the Giralda climb works

The tower was raised between 1184 and 1198 as the minaret of the great mosque, a sister of the Koutoubia in Marrakesh. Its builders did not put stairs inside. They built ramps: thirty-five of them, wide and gently sloped, turning around the core of the tower, so that the man who gave the call to prayer could go up on horseback.

For a visitor that has practical consequences.

  • There is no lift, and no other way up or down.
  • It is easier than a staircase. You walk uphill for about ten to fifteen minutes. The ramps are numbered, so you always know how far you have come, and windows on every side let you stop for breath and for the view.
  • Only the last stretch is steps: a short flight from the top ramp up into the bell chamber.
  • The same ramps serve both directions. In the middle of the day people going up squeeze past people coming down, and the bell chamber itself is crowded.
  • The bells are real. They hang just above your head and they ring.

The bell chamber and everything above it are Christian additions of the 1560s, by the architect Hernán Ruiz. On the very top turns a bronze figure of Faith that works as a weathervane. The people of Seville called it the Giraldillo, from the verb for turning, and the tower took its name from it. A full-size copy stands outside the cathedral, so you can see how big it is.

The Court of the Orange Trees, the courtyard of the old mosque, from the Giralda. Photo: Jebulon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Seville from the Giralda. Photo: Benjamin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What to look for inside

  • The tomb of Columbus. Four figures larger than life, dressed as heralds of the kingdoms of Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre, carry his coffin on their shoulders. The monument was made for the cathedral of Havana and came to Seville in 1899, after Spain lost Cuba.
  • The high altar. Behind a tall iron screen rises a wall of carved and gilded wood with dozens of scenes from the life of Christ. The Flemish sculptor Pieter Dancart began it in 1482 and it took three generations to finish. It is usually called the largest altarpiece in Christendom.
  • The paintings. The sacristies hold works by Murillo and Zurbarán, and Goya's canvas of Seville's patron saints, Justa and Rufina, with the Giralda between them.

The tomb of Columbus, carried by the heralds of four Spanish kingdoms. Photo: José Luiz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What is sold separately

  • The rooftop visit. The cathedral runs guided walks over its roofs, among the buttresses and pinnacles. They have their own ticket, fixed times and limited places. A general ticket does not include them.
  • The Alcázar. The royal palace is across the square, a different monument with a different owner, ticket and line.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A cathedral and Giralda ticket is timed entry to the church and the tower. The partner's plain ticket also lists the Church of El Salvador.
  • A ticket and audio tour with a city walk adds commentary in the partner's app on your phone, inside the cathedral and on a walk through the centre afterwards. Bring earphones.
  • An audio tour marked "without a ticket" is commentary only. You buy your entry separately.
  • The audio tour of the cathedral, the Giralda and the Alcázar covers three monuments and includes a ticket to none of them. It is a guide for people who already hold their tickets.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for Seville Cathedral and the Giralda, with today's prices:

[partner q="giralda" match="cathedral,giralda" limit="6"]

Practical notes

  • Allow an hour and a half for the cathedral and the tower together, and half an hour more for El Salvador.
  • Go up the tower first if you arrive at opening time, before the ramps fill, and see the church afterwards.
  • This is a working cathedral. On Sundays and feast days visits start later, after the morning services, and chapels can close without notice.
  • Dress as you would for any church in use: shoulders covered, no beachwear.
  • In summer the ramps are warm by midday. Bring water.

Hours change with the season and the church calendar. The current ones are on our pages for Seville Cathedral and the Giralda.

From here

You come out through the Court of the Orange Trees on the north side. The Alcázar of Seville is two minutes away across the Plaza del Triunfo, and between the two stands the Archive of the Indies, which keeps the papers of Spain's American empire. Behind the Alcázar wall begin the lanes of the Santa Cruz quarter, the old Jewish district. For the rest of Seville, or to see what lies around it, open the attractions map of Spain.

Cover photo: Heinz Joerg Kretschmer, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

faqs.q: Is the Giralda included in the Seville Cathedral ticket?
faqs.a: Yes. A general ticket to the cathedral includes the climb up the Giralda. There is no separate ticket for the tower.

faqs.q: How do you climb the Giralda?
faqs.a: On foot, up 35 gently sloped ramps that turn around the inside of the tower, followed by a short flight of steps into the bell chamber. It takes about ten to fifteen minutes.

faqs.q: Is there a lift in the Giralda?
faqs.a: No. The ramps are the only way up and down, and they are shared by people going in both directions.

faqs.q: Where is Columbus buried in Seville Cathedral?
faqs.a: His tomb stands inside the cathedral, near the south door: a coffin carried by four large figures representing the kingdoms of Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to Seville Cathedral take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for the cathedral and the Giralda together. Add half an hour if you also use the ticket for the Church of El Salvador.

title: Royal Alcázar of Seville: how to avoid the queue, and what the ticket covers
subtitle: One gate, a limit on visitors, and an upper floor that a general ticket does not open.
excerpt: Why there is a line at the Lion Gate of the Alcázar of Seville and how to stay out of it, what a general ticket covers in the palaces and gardens, and what the royal apartments upstairs require.
focus_keyword: Alcázar of Seville avoid the queue
longtail_phrases: how to skip the line at the Alcázar of Seville
do you need to book the Alcázar of Seville in advance
what does the Alcázar of Seville ticket include
are the royal apartments included in the Alcázar ticket
how long does the Alcázar of Seville take
meta_title: Alcázar of Seville: avoid the queue, what the ticket covers
meta_description: Why there is a line at the Alcázar of Seville, how to stay out of it, what a general ticket covers and why the royal apartments upstairs are extra.

featured_image.alt: The Courtyard of the Maidens in the Alcázar of Seville, with a long pool between sunken gardens and carved arcades

content_html:
[place attraction="alcazar-of-seville" city="seville"]

In 1364 a Christian king of Castile began a new palace inside the old fortress of Seville, and built it in the manner of his Muslim neighbours. Peter I, called the Cruel by his enemies and the Just by his friends, was an ally of the ruler of Granada, and craftsmen from Granada and Toledo worked on his walls alongside those of Seville. They covered them in Arabic. The inscriptions praise the sultan Don Pedro, and repeat the motto of the kings of Granada: there is no victor but God.

The palace has been a royal residence ever since. The king of Spain still stays on its upper floor when he is in Seville, which makes it one of the oldest palaces in Europe that is still lived in. It is also a place with one visitor gate and a limit on how many people may be inside, and that combination produces the best-known queue in Andalusia.

The Lion Gate, the entrance for every visitor. The square in front is rarely this empty. Photo: José Luis Filpo Cabana, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Why there is a queue

Everybody enters by the Lion Gate, the red gateway on the Plaza del Triunfo, opposite the cathedral. Entry is sold by time slot. People who arrive without a ticket stand in a line for whatever is left that day, in the sun, and in spring and autumn there is often nothing left.

With a ticket bought in advance you go to the gate at your time. You will still wait a few minutes, because everyone passes a bag check, but that is all.

How to stay out of it

  • Book days ahead, and weeks ahead for Holy Week, the April Fair and any long weekend.
  • Take the first slot of the morning or one in the last two hours. The coach groups fill the hours from eleven to two.
  • Arrive ten minutes before your time, not an hour. Turning up early does not get you in early.
  • Bring the identity document you booked with. The Alcázar issues tickets in the visitor's name, and the staff at the gate can ask to see it.

What a general ticket covers

The general ticket opens the whole ground floor and the gardens, which is nearly everything.

  • The Palace of Peter I. The Courtyard of the Maidens, with a sunken garden down its middle that archaeologists found under a marble floor in the early 2000s. The Hall of Ambassadors, under a dome of gilded and interlaced wood made in 1427. The small Courtyard of the Dolls, for the private side of the house.
  • The House of Trade. From 1503 the voyages to the Americas were run from these rooms. In its chapel hangs the Virgin of the Navigators, painted in the 1530s, with ships at her feet.
  • The Gothic Palace of the thirteenth century, later given tiled walls and a set of huge tapestries of Charles V's campaign in Tunis. The emperor married Isabella of Portugal in the Alcázar in 1526.
  • The Baths of María de Padilla. Not baths at all: rainwater tanks under a courtyard, a long vaulted hall with still water down the middle.
  • The gardens, which are as big a part of the visit as the rooms: the Mercury Pond, the Grotto Gallery built onto an old defensive wall that you can walk along, orange and palm trees, fountains, a maze, and peacocks.

The dome of the Hall of Ambassadors, made in 1427. Photo: José Luis Filpo Cabana, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The Baths of María de Padilla: rainwater tanks under a courtyard. Photo: Tesla Delacroix, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What it does not cover

The royal apartments upstairs, the Cuarto Real Alto. These are the rooms the royal family uses, and they are visited separately: an extra ticket for a fixed time, a small group, an audio guide, bags left in a locker. Places are few and go first. They also close when the family is in residence. If you want them, look for the words on the listing or ask at the gate, and expect to hear that the day is full.

The general ticket does not include the cathedral either. The two monuments face each other across the square and have nothing else in common.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A general admission ticket is timed entry to the ground floor and the gardens. The partner's own listing states that the royal rooms upstairs are not included.
  • A ticket and audio tour of the palace is the same entry with commentary in the partner's app on your phone. There are few explanations on the walls of the Alcázar, so a guide of some kind adds a lot. Bring earphones.
  • An audio tour marked "without a ticket" is the commentary alone.
  • The audio tour of the cathedral, the Giralda and the Alcázar covers all three and includes entry to none.

These are the Alcázar tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner q="alcazar seville" match="alcazar" limit="6"]

How long, and in what order

Allow two hours, and two and a half if you like gardens. A good order is to go straight through the first courtyards to the Palace of Peter I while it is quiet, then the Gothic Palace and the baths below it, and to leave the gardens for last, when you no longer mind the time.

From June to September the gardens are hot by noon and the tiled rooms are the cool part: reverse the order if your slot is late in the morning. Opening hours are shorter in winter. The current ones are on our page for the Alcázar of Seville.

The Grotto Gallery above the Mercury Pond, where the gardens begin. Photo: Anual, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

From here

The way out leads through the Patio de Banderas, a quiet square of orange trees with a framed view of the Giralda. A covered passage in its corner leads into the lanes of the Santa Cruz quarter. Seville Cathedral is two minutes in the other direction, and the Plaza de España is a fifteen-minute walk south, past the old tobacco factory that is now the university. See what else there is in Seville, or build a route through Andalusia with the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Benjamin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How do you avoid the queue at the Alcázar of Seville?
faqs.a: Buy a ticket for a time slot in advance and arrive about ten minutes before it. The long line at the Lion Gate is for people without a ticket. The first slot of the morning and the last two hours are the calmest.

faqs.q: Do you need to book the Alcázar of Seville in advance?
faqs.a: In practice, yes. Entry is by time slot and numbers are limited, so in spring, in autumn and on holidays the day often sells out before you reach the ticket window.

faqs.q: What does a general ticket to the Alcázar of Seville include?
faqs.a: The whole ground floor and the gardens: the Palace of Peter I with the Courtyard of the Maidens and the Hall of Ambassadors, the House of Trade, the Gothic Palace and the Baths of María de Padilla.

faqs.q: Are the royal apartments included in the Alcázar ticket?
faqs.a: No. The upper floor, the Cuarto Real Alto, is visited with a separate timed ticket in a small group, and places are limited. It closes when the royal family is staying.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Alcázar of Seville take?
faqs.a: About two hours for the palaces and the gardens, and up to two and a half if you walk the gardens at leisure.

title: Pena Palace from Lisbon: how to get there, and palace or park ticket?
subtitle: A train, a hill, a second hill inside the gate, and a time on your ticket that means the palace door.
excerpt: How to reach Pena Palace in Sintra from Lisbon without a car, how long each stage takes, what the time on the ticket refers to, and when the park ticket is enough.
secondary_keywords: how to get to Pena Palace
longtail_phrases: how to get to Pena Palace from Lisbon by train
is the Pena Palace interior worth it
what is the difference between the Pena park and palace ticket
how long is the walk from the Pena gate to the palace

meta_title: Pena Palace from Lisbon: getting there, palace or park
meta_description: How to reach Pena Palace from Lisbon by train and bus, what the time on your ticket means, and whether to buy the palace or the park ticket.

featured_image.alt: Pena Palace in Sintra, with its yellow domed tower, grey tiled wing and red clock tower above the trees

content_html:
[place attraction="pena-palace" city="sintra"]

In 1836 a German prince of nineteen, Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, arrived in Lisbon to marry Queen Maria II of Portugal. Two years later he bought, with his own money, a ruin on a peak above the town of Sintra: a small monastery founded by King Manuel I in 1503 and wrecked by the great earthquake of 1755. He gave the job of rebuilding it to Baron von Eschwege, a German mining engineer, and for more than a decade the two of them added towers, domes, a drawbridge and a tunnel of an entrance around what was left of the cloister.

The result is the red and yellow palace on every poster of Portugal. It stands nearly five hundred metres above the sea, on top of a wooded hill, at the end of a narrow road. The palace is easy to love and awkward to reach, and most of what goes wrong on a day trip here goes wrong before the front door.

Lisbon to Sintra

Take the train. The Sintra line starts at Rossio station in the centre of Lisbon, runs several times an hour and takes about forty minutes. Sintra is the last stop, so you cannot miss it. Buy your ticket before boarding and keep it for the gates at the other end.

Do not drive. The roads up the hill are narrow and one-way, traffic around the old town is restricted, and there is almost nowhere to park near the palace.

Sintra station, the last stop of the line from Lisbon. Photo: Andrzej Otrębski, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Sintra station to the palace gate

The gate of the park is about three and a half kilometres from the station and a long way above it.

  • Bus 434 runs a one-way loop: the station, the old town, the Castle of the Moors, Pena, and back down. In high season the line for it at the station can be long by mid-morning.
  • A taxi, a ride-hailing car or a tuk-tuk costs more and saves the wait. Agree where you will be dropped: the main gate is the one you want.
  • On foot, a marked path climbs from the old town through the woods in about an hour. It is steep and shaded, and a good way to come down.

The palace on its peak, seen from the Castle of the Moors. Everything below it is the park. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The time on your ticket

This is the detail that catches people. The inside of the palace is visited by time slot, and the time printed on your ticket is the time at the door of the palace, not at the gate of the park.

Between the two there is a second climb: a steep ten to fifteen minutes on foot through the gardens, or a short ride on a small shuttle that is paid for separately. Add the check at the gate, and you should be walking into the park at least half an hour before your slot. If your train or your bus runs late and you miss the time, the staff are entitled to refuse you.

So work backwards. For a slot at eleven, be at the gate by half past ten, on a bus by ten, and on a train out of Lisbon before nine.

Palace or park ticket?

There are two kinds of ticket, and the cheaper one is not a mistake.

  • Palace and park gets you inside the building at your time slot, and into the whole park before and after.
  • Park only has no time slot. You walk the grounds and see the palace from outside, close enough to touch its walls. It has also let visitors onto the outer terraces of the palace: check that this is written on the ticket you buy.

What do you get inside? The cloister of the old monastery, lined with tiles. Its chapel, with an altarpiece in alabaster and black marble carved around 1530. And a chain of small royal rooms kept as the family left them, down to the kitchen and its copper pans: the last queen of Portugal spent her final night in the country here in October 1910. The rooms are narrow, the route is one-way, and on a busy day you shuffle through in a slow line.

Outside is the part everyone photographs: the coloured walls, the Triton archway, the wall walk with its views to the Atlantic, and a park of some eighty-five hectares that Ferdinand planted with trees from every continent. The High Cross, a viewpoint on the top of the Sintra hills, looks back at the palace from above.

The Triton above the archway into the palace. Photo: Husond, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

  • Choose the palace ticket if you like royal interiors, if you are here on a quiet weekday or out of season, or if this is your one palace in Portugal.
  • Choose the park ticket if you are short of time, travelling with small children, visiting on a summer weekend, or cannot get a time slot that fits your trains.

Red for the old monastery, yellow for the palace built around it. Photo: Chabe01, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A palace entrance ticket is entry at a set time. Read which areas are listed.
  • A ticket with an audio tour adds a guide in the partner's app on your phone. One version covers the palace; another names both the palace and the park. Bring earphones.
  • A priority entrance ticket. Open its "included" section before you pay more for the word priority, and make sure something is written there.
  • An audio tour on its own is commentary only, with no entry.

Several of these are listed twice, once under Sintra and once under Lisbon. A title that begins with Lisbon does not mean transport from Lisbon: none of these products includes the train or the bus.

These are the Pena Palace tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="pena-palace" match="pena" limit="6"]

When to go

  • The first slot of the day, reached by an early train, is the only one without a crowd in summer. Late afternoon is second best.
  • Sintra has its own weather. The hill can sit in cloud and wind while Lisbon is in sunshine, so bring a layer, and do not count on the view.
  • Weekends and Portuguese public holidays are the busiest days.

Opening hours and last entries change with the season. The current ones are on our page for Pena Palace.

From here

The Castle of the Moors is a ten-minute walk downhill from the Pena gate, a line of ruined walls along a ridge with a ticket of its own. Down in the town are the National Palace with its two white chimneys and, a short walk beyond it, Quinta da Regaleira with its spiral well. Three sights are too many for one day: choose two. See what else there is in Sintra, or plan the days around it with the trip planner for Portugal.

Cover photo: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to Pena Palace from Lisbon?
faqs.a: Take the train from Rossio station in Lisbon to Sintra, the last stop, in about forty minutes. From Sintra station take bus 434, a taxi or a tuk-tuk up to the gate of the park, or walk up in about an hour.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the palace ticket and the park ticket at Pena?
faqs.a: The palace and park ticket lets you inside the building at a set time, as well as into the grounds. The park ticket covers the grounds only, with the palace seen from outside, and has no time slot.

faqs.q: What does the time on a Pena Palace ticket mean?
faqs.a: It is the time at the door of the palace, not at the gate of the park. The walk between the two is steep and takes ten to fifteen minutes, so enter the park at least half an hour earlier.

faqs.q: Is the inside of Pena Palace worth it?
faqs.a: It is if you like royal interiors and can visit at a quiet time. The rooms are small and the route is a slow one-way line on busy days. The best-known views of the palace are all outside.

faqs.q: Can you walk from Sintra station to Pena Palace?
faqs.a: Yes. A marked path climbs from the old town through the woods in about an hour. It is steep, so many visitors ride up and walk down.

title: Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres: a day trip from Barcelona by train, and which ticket
subtitle: Two stations, two kinds of train, one timed ticket, and a museum that explains nothing on purpose.
excerpt: How to reach the Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres from Barcelona by train, which of the two stations to use, what the ticket includes, what it does not, and how to fill the day.
focus_keyword: Dalí Museum Figueres day trip from Barcelona
longtail_phrases: how to get from Barcelona to the Dalí Museum in Figueres

meta_title: Dalí Museum Figueres: day trip from Barcelona by train
meta_description: Barcelona to the Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres by train: which station, how long, what the ticket includes and how to plan the day.

featured_image.alt: The red tower of the Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres, topped with giant eggs, with the glass dome behind it

content_html:
[place attraction="dali-theatre-and-museum" city="figueres"]

In 1961 the mayor of Figueres asked the most famous man ever born in the town to give a painting to its museum. Salvador Dalí answered that he would give a whole museum, and he chose the place himself: the shell of the municipal theatre, burned out at the end of the Civil War. It was where, at fourteen, he had hung his pictures in public for the first time. The Theatre-Museum opened in September 1974.

Dalí spent his last years in the tower next door and died there in January 1989. He is buried under the old stage, beneath the glass dome. In 2017 a court had the tomb opened to settle a paternity claim. The claim turned out to be false, and the embalmer reported that the moustache was still in place, pointing at ten past ten.

All of this is 140 kilometres from Barcelona, which makes it the classic day trip from the city. It works well by train, as long as you know that Figueres has two stations.

The glass dome over the old stage, and the eggs along the roof. Photo: Maksim Sokolov, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Is it worth a day?

Know what the place is first. It is not a gallery of Dalí's best-known canvases: the melting watches are in New York. It is a single large work that he designed room by room, and he called it a theatre for a reason.

  • The courtyard, where the stalls used to be, holds a black Cadillac in which it rains on the passengers.
  • One room is a living room when you walk in and the face of the actress Mae West when you climb a few steps and look back.
  • A huge canvas on the stage shows his wife Gala from behind, looking at the sea. Step back twenty metres and it becomes a portrait of Abraham Lincoln.
  • Among the tricks hang real paintings from every decade of his life, the early ones included.

There are almost no labels, because Dalí wanted none. If you like to understand what you are looking at, that is the argument for a guide in your ear.

Barcelona to Figueres: two trains, two stations

  • The high-speed train leaves from Barcelona Sants and reaches Figueres Vilafant in a little under an hour. Seats are reserved and the cheap fares go early, so book ahead. Vilafant station stands in fields on the western edge of the town: the museum is about twenty minutes away on foot, or a short ride by bus or taxi.
  • The regional train leaves from Sants and also stops at Passeig de Gràcia. It takes around two hours, costs much less and needs no reservation. It arrives at the old station, called simply Figueres, on the eastern side of the centre. From there the museum is a walk of ten to fifteen minutes, by way of the Rambla.

The two stations are on opposite sides of town and about half an hour's walk apart. Before you leave the museum, check which one your return train uses. A common plan is fast out and slow back, or the reverse.

By car the journey takes about an hour and a half on the motorway, and parking in the centre is paid.

A high-speed train at Figueres Vilafant, the station outside the town. Photo: mike, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

What the ticket includes

Entry is for a set time. In July and August, and on rainy days when the whole coast comes inland, the slots sell out, so buy before you buy the train.

The museum ticket also covers Dalí Jewels, a separate set of rooms with its own door around the corner: a few dozen pieces in gold and precious stones that he designed between the 1940s and 1970, among them a ruby heart that beats. Many visitors leave without knowing it was included. Keep your ticket and allow twenty minutes.

It does not cover the other two Dalí sites, which are not in Figueres at all:

  • His house at Portlligat, beside Cadaqués on the coast, about an hour away by road. It is visited in very small groups at a booked time, and fills up long in advance.
  • The castle at Púbol, which he gave to Gala, in the countryside towards Girona.

Neither is easy without a car, and neither fits comfortably into the same day as Figueres from Barcelona.

The front of the old theatre, and the line for the door. Photo: Jordiferrer, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • An entrance ticket is timed entry to the Theatre-Museum. The partner's listing names the Jewels as included.
  • A ticket and audio tour adds commentary in the partner's app on your own phone, room by room. Bring earphones.
  • An audio tour with a town walk comes in two versions with nearly the same name. One includes entry. The other states plainly that the museum ticket is not included. Read which one you have in the basket.

None of them includes the train.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for the Dalí Theatre-Museum, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="dali-theatre-and-museum" match="dali" limit="6"]

A plan for the day

  • Morning. A train that gets you to Figueres about an hour before your slot. Walk around the outside of the building first: the red walls studded with loaves of bread and the giant eggs on the roof are half the show, and they are free.
  • Late morning. The museum. Allow two hours, then the Jewels.
  • Lunch on or near the Rambla, the tree-lined promenade at the bottom of the old town.
  • Afternoon. Sant Ferran Castle, an enormous eighteenth-century fortress on the hill above the museum, is a fifteen-minute walk and usually almost empty.

The museum closes on most Mondays outside the summer months. Check the current days and hours on our page for the Dalí Theatre-Museum before you book a train.

The Rambla of Figueres, between the old station and the museum. Photo: Zarateman, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

From here

Both kinds of train stop in Girona on the way back, forty kilometres south, and its old town and cathedral are well worth breaking the journey for a couple of hours. If you are staying in the north, see what else is close to Figueres. If you are going back to the city, here is what there is to do in Barcelona, and the attractions map of Spain shows the rest.

Cover photo: Enfo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: How do you get from Barcelona to the Dalí Museum in Figueres?
faqs.a: By train. The high-speed train from Barcelona Sants reaches Figueres Vilafant in a little under an hour, and the regional train reaches the old Figueres station in around two hours. The museum is a walk from either.

faqs.q: Which Figueres station is closer to the Dalí Museum?
faqs.a: The old station, called Figueres, used by regional trains: ten to fifteen minutes on foot. Figueres Vilafant, the high-speed station, is about twenty minutes on foot or a short bus or taxi ride.

faqs.q: Is the Dalí Museum in Figueres worth a day trip from Barcelona?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want to see a building Dalí designed as one large work, with its optical tricks and installations. It is not the place to see his most famous canvases, several of which are in other countries.

faqs.q: Does the Dalí Theatre-Museum ticket include the Dalí Jewels?
faqs.a: Yes. The jewels are shown in separate rooms with their own door around the corner, and the same ticket lets you in.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the Dalí Theatre-Museum?
faqs.a: About two hours for the museum and twenty minutes for the Jewels. With the train from Barcelona it fills most of a day.
